assessmentSummary.identity: A bilateral vertical jump initiated from a motionless partial-squat hold, followed by a bilateral landing in the takeoff area and a deliberate two-second stick.
currentCardFindings: The legacy card does not specify a pause, so it overlaps the separate Countermovement Jump to Stick identity.
Its generic 40-point scoring understates impact and failure consequence while leaving supervision, impact, and work-capacity demand unscored.
Anatomy, controlled taxonomy, load, fatigue, constraints, and support fields are empty; one repetition at RPE 9 does not define start depth, pause, jump intent, landing hold, or progression.

proposedDosage.progressWhen: the athlete holds the same squat depth, jumps without a countermovement, and lands quietly in the takeoff area on every repetition

coachCues: Set the squat depth and become still
Jump straight up without dipping again
athleteInstructions: Hold a shallow squat for two seconds
Jump straight up from the still position
Land on both feet and hold

readiness: mastered snap-down and basic bilateral jump landing

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Rename to Paused Squat Jump to Stick or require a two-to-three-second static start in every profile. The separate countermovement card owns a rapid dip-and-drive; do not treat the two starts as interchangeable.

currentCardSnapshot.description: The athlete performs Squat Jump to Stick as a quality-first jump-height drill, emphasizing connects basic vertical force production to landing ownership so athletes do not separate takeoff height from safe finish position.

evidence.sourceTitle: Basics of Strength and Conditioning Manual
claims: Jump identity must distinguish the starting action, projection direction, takeoff and landing laterality, external height or obstacle, rebound intent, and required stabilization.
Squat Jump to Stick must not combine a paused static start, countermovement, repeated rebound, loaded jump, testing protocol, or different landing laterality under one unspecified card.
A jump-to-stick combines ballistic propulsion with a deliberate landing and stabilization phase; repeated reactive hopping is a different programming task.
Squat Jump to Stick belongs to jump power with landing control, with direction, laterality, initiation, flight action, and rebound intent encoded as controlled dimensions.
Propulsion and force absorption are coordinated across the foot and ankle, knee, hip, pelvis, and trunk.

The card should assign task-specific roles to plantar flexors and intrinsic foot muscles, quadriceps, hamstrings, gluteals, hip stabilizers, and trunk stabilizers rather than naming one isolated muscle.

evidence.sourceTitle: Basics of Strength and Conditioning Manual
claims: Jump demand changes with projection speed, direction, external height, body mass, and the time available to produce and absorb force.

Observable quality includes the prescribed initiation, coordinated ankle-knee-hip propulsion, intended flight path, re-extension before contact where needed, quiet whole-foot landing, knee tracking, trunk control, and ownership of the finish.

evidence.sourceTitle: Basics of Strength and Conditioning Manual
claims: Plyometric intensity changes with speed, height, distance, body mass, external load, laterality, and movement complexity.

Exercise difficulty must score technical complexity and physical demand directly, including coordination, impact, supervision, work capacity, and consequence of error; an exercise card must not receive a skill-library level.

evidence.sourceTitle: Basics of Strength and Conditioning Manual
claims: Landing contacts, jump height or distance, approach and initiation, laterality, and external load govern mechanical exposure; high-quality power repetitions require adequate rest.

Squat Jump to Stick needs contact count, intent, impact and eccentric stress, technical-fatigue sensitivity, performance-loss criteria, and recovery guidance instead of treating all jumps as conditioning repetitions.

evidence.sourceTitle: Training interventions to reduce the risk of injury to the lower extremity joints during landing movements in adult athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
claims: Effective jump-landing interventions depend on appropriate materials, coaching knowledge, usable space, and task-specific progression.

The delivery profile should require a level non-slip surface, clear flight and landing zones, adequate ceiling height, suitable footwear, athlete spacing, coach sightline, and readiness for the prescribed landing demand.
Landing and stabilization control should precede higher, farther, unilateral, repeated, or reactive jumping.
Prescribe low-repetition quality sets, contacts, intent, target height or distance where relevant, hold duration, rest, and progression criteria; stop before fatigue alters takeoff or landing.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Use of Augmented Information for Reducing Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk During Jump Landings: A Systematic Review
claims: Specific prescriptive feedback can improve jump-landing mechanics, while excessive cue volume can interfere with learning.
Use a small cue set tied to the identity: perform the prescribed start, project in the intended direction, land quietly, align foot-knee-hip, and hold without a touch-down, shuffle, or rebound.
Loud contact, poor stabilization, loss of alignment, or inability to coordinate ankle, knee, and hip indicate that jump intensity or volume exceeds current control.
Stop for pain, giving way, dizziness, repeated valgus or trunk collapse, uncontrolled foot contact, failure to re-extend before landing, missed landing zone, extra steps, or loss of jump output.

evidence.sourceTitle: Evidence-Based Best-Practice Guidelines for Preventing Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries in Young Female Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
evidence.sourcePublisher: The American Journal of Sports Medicine
claims: Landing stabilization and lower-body strength are recurring components of effective neuromuscular injury-prevention programs.
Squat Jump to Stick belongs after preparation and before fatigued conditioning; high-intent jump work should use low volume and full enough recovery to preserve output and landing quality.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Use of Augmented Information for Reducing Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk During Jump Landings: A Systematic Review
claims: Athletes benefit from feedback tied to visible movement actions rather than abstract risk language.
Athlete support should show the start, flight, and landing shapes, define a successful repetition, identify the target and hold time, provide one primary cue, and explain the stop signal.

evidence.sourceTitle: Training interventions to reduce the risk of injury to the lower extremity joints during landing movements in adult athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
claims: Coach education and practical implementation affect whether jump-landing interventions are delivered effectively.

Coach support should provide front and side observation points, pass-fail criteria, contact counting, output-loss and asymmetry rules, progressions, regressions, equipment checks, and rules for reducing height, distance, laterality, or cue complexity.
Beginners should establish bilateral landing and stabilization before progressing to unilateral, higher, farther, or reactive tasks.

Accessibility can be improved with visual targets, demonstrated shapes, plain-language cues, reduced height or distance, assistance, longer reset time, and reduced sensory or decision load without assigning an exercise skill level.

evidence.sourceTitle: Basics of Strength and Conditioning Manual
claims: Static starts, countermovements, jumps covering distance, unilateral landings, repeated contacts, obstacles, and externally loaded jumps have different intensity and programming implications.

Arm action, target distance, submaximal intent, and assistance are usually variants or modifiers; different initiation, projection, landing laterality, rebound intent, or testing purpose may require a distinct definition.

alternateAssessments.name: Paused Squat Jump to Stick
alternateAssessments.rationale: The pause makes the intended static-start identity explicit and separates it from a countermovement jump.

alternateAssessments.name: Countermovement Jump to Stick
alternateAssessments.rationale: A rapid eccentric dip before takeoff changes initiation, stretch-shortening contribution, and timing demand.

alternateAssessments.name: Arm-Restricted Paused Squat Jump
alternateAssessments.rationale: Hands-on-hips execution changes arm contribution but preserves the static bilateral vertical jump.

alternateAssessments.name: Band-Assisted Squat Jump to Stick
alternateAssessments.rationale: Assistance reduces effective load and landing demand while preserving the start and projection.

alternateAssessments.name: Repeated Jump Squats
alternateAssessments.rationale: Continuous rebounds remove the stick and emphasize reactive output or work capacity.
